blocks.text: Bacteria use different motility patterns to navigate and explore their natural habitats. The textbook describes six: flagellar movement, twitching (crawling), gliding, sliding, Brownian movement and movement by an axial filament.

Most bacilli and spirilla move by means of flagella: they swim. When a whole bacterial population moves together by means of flagella, the movement is called swarming. Flagellar movement lets bacteria travel in liquid media. Counter-clockwise rotation of the flagellum pushes the cell forward with the flagellum trailing behind.
Twitching is used to move over surfaces. It is mediated by pili, which bind to the surrounding solid surface and then retract, so the bacterial cell is pulled forward.
Gliding is similar to twitching. In gliding, bacteria secrete a slimy substance that helps them glide smoothly over solid surfaces.
Sliding is due to the expansion created by the pushing force of dividing cells.
Some bacteria that have neither flagella nor pili, such as Streptococcus, move because of the random and uncontrolled movements of the particles in the fluid around them.

Some bacteria, the spirochaetes, have a modified flagellum known as an axial filament. It is anchored at one end and runs lengthwise in the periplasmic space (between the cell membrane and the outer membrane). It consists of two sets of flagella-like fibrils anchored at the two poles of the cell. The axial filament helps spirochaetes with flexing, swimming, creeping and spinning movements.

blocks.alt: A long spiral spirochaete cell. Inside its outer sheath, two sets of fibrils run lengthwise from each pole along the periplasmic space, overlapping in the middle.

blocks.long_description: The cell is a wavy spiral enclosed by an outer membrane. The cell body is drawn inside it. Between the two, in the periplasmic space, fibrils anchored at the left pole run to the right and fibrils anchored at the right pole run to the left, so they overlap along the middle of the cell. Labels mark the outer membrane, the periplasmic space, the cell body and the two sets of fibrils.

blocks.prompt: How do twitching and gliding differ, and what does Brownian movement tell you about a bacterium's appendages?
blocks.explanation: Twitching uses pili that bind to a surface and retract to pull the cell; gliding uses secreted slime for smooth movement over a surface. Brownian movement is not self-propelled: it happens in bacteria without flagella or pili, moved by random fluid particles.

items: Flagellar movement: swimming in liquid; swarming when a population moves together; counter-clockwise rotation pushes the cell forward.
Twitching uses pili (bind and retract); gliding uses slime; sliding comes from dividing cells pushing.
Brownian movement is passive, in bacteria without flagella or pili.
Spirochaetes use an axial filament, a modified flagellum in the periplasmic space, for flexing, swimming, creeping and spinning.
